warmup.text_pt: "**Google**" virou verbo. "**Brunch**" é breakfast + lunch. "**Selfie**" foi palavra do ano do Oxford Dictionaries em 2013. A cada ano, milhares de palavras novas surgem em inglês — e algumas entram nos dicionários. No C2, você precisa **entender neologismos na hora**, reconhecendo os **mecanismos** que os criam, e saber **quando** usá-los.
questions: Which English words have entered Portuguese recently? Do you use them?
Can you think of a word that didn't exist ten years ago?

grammar.title: How new words are made
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Blends (palavras-valise)** — partes de duas palavras:
- brunch (breakfast + lunch), smog (smoke + fog), motel (motor + hotel), podcast (iPod + broadcast), staycation (stay + vacation), Brexit (Britain + exit), infodemic (information + epidemic)

**2. Conversão** — a palavra muda de **classe** sem mudar de forma:
- substantivo → verbo: **to google**, **to text**, **to email**, **to friend**, **to adult** (informal), **to gift**
- verbo → substantivo: **an ask** ("a big ask"), **a read** ("a good read"), **a must-have**, **a fail**
- adjetivo → verbo: **to green** (a cidade), **to empty**

**3. Afixos produtivos:**
- **-ify / -ize**: gamify, monetize, weaponize, Uberize
- **-esque / -ian**: Kafkaesque, Orwellian, Dickensian (como na obra de...)
- **-ism / -ist**: ageism, lookism, ableism
- **-ish**: sevenish, greenish, "Are you happy?" "**Ish.**" (informal)
- **-ee / -er**: trainee, influencer
- **hyper- / mega- / post- / micro- / e- / cyber-**: hyperlocal, mega-rich, post-truth, microplastics, e-learning, cybercrime
- **un-** criativo: unfriend, unfollow, unsend

**4. Compostos:** deepfake, doomscrolling, screen time, side hustle, cancel culture

**5. Siglas:**
- **Acronym** (lido como palavra): NASA, laser (light amplification by...), FOMO, YOLO
- **Initialism** (soletrada): FAQ, DIY, BBC

**6. Back-formation** — criar uma palavra "mais simples" a partir de uma mais longa: **edit** (de editor), **babysit** (de babysitter), **donate** (de donation), **burgle** (de burglar)

**7. Empréstimos:** emoji (japonês), tsunami, schadenfreude (alemão), hygge (dinamarquês) — e do português: **samba, caipirinha, favela, capoeira, piranha**.

**Registro:** neologismos informais (ghosting, adulting) funcionam na fala e em textos leves; em textos formais, prefira termos estabelecidos ou explique o neologismo ("so-called 'doomscrolling'").

dialogue.title: The generation gap
dialogue.context_pt: Uma avó pergunta à neta o significado de palavras que ela ouve no trabalho e nas redes.

lines.speaker: Grandma
lines.en: Bia, your cousin said she was "ghosted". Did she see a ghost?
lines.pt: Bia, sua prima disse que foi "ghosted". Ela viu um fantasma?

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: Ha! No, Grandma. It means a guy she was dating just disappeared — stopped answering messages without any explanation.
lines.pt: Ha! Não, vó. Significa que um cara com quem ela estava saindo simplesmente sumiu — parou de responder mensagens sem explicação.

lines.speaker: Grandma
lines.en: Ah. In my day we just called that being rude. And "doomscrolling"? Your father says he's been doing it.
lines.pt: Ah. No meu tempo a gente chamava isso só de falta de educação. E "doomscrolling"? Seu pai diz que anda fazendo isso.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: That's scrolling through bad news on your phone for hours. "Doom" plus "scrolling". People started using it a lot during the pandemic.
lines.pt: É ficar rolando notícias ruins no celular por horas. "Doom" mais "scrolling". As pessoas começaram a usar muito durante a pandemia.

lines.speaker: Grandma
lines.en: These words appear from nowhere! When I was young, nobody "googled" anything. We went to the library.
lines.pt: Essas palavras aparecem do nada! Quando eu era jovem, ninguém "googlava" nada. A gente ia à biblioteca.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: But you invented words too! Didn't you tell me "smog" was new once?
lines.pt: Mas vocês também inventavam palavras! Você não me disse que "smog" já foi novidade?

lines.speaker: Grandma
lines.en: That was before my time, cheeky! But you're right. Language never stops changing.
lines.pt: Isso foi antes do meu tempo, sua atrevida! Mas você tem razão. A língua nunca para de mudar.

lines.speaker: Bia
lines.en: Exactly. Now, can I teach you what "FOMO" means?
lines.pt: Exatamente. Agora, posso te ensinar o que significa "FOMO"?

listening.title: How a word gets into the dictionary
listening.context_pt: Uma lexicógrafa explica como os dicionários decidem incluir palavras novas.

lines.speaker: Lexicographer
lines.en: People often ask me who decides whether a word is "real". The honest answer is: nobody — and everybody. Dictionaries of English don't create words, and they don't approve them. They observe them. Lexicographers track huge collections of real language — books, newspapers, websites, transcripts — looking for words that are being used widely, by many different people, over a sustained period. A word that appears once in a viral post and then disappears won't make it. But if a word keeps appearing in different contexts, across different types of writing, for several years, it's likely to be added. That's how words like "selfie", "emoji" and "podcast" found their way into major dictionaries. This is quite different from languages that have official academies — Portuguese and French, for example, have institutions that publish official vocabularies or spelling rules. English has never had an equivalent. Its dictionaries are descriptive: they tell you how people actually use the language, not how they ought to.

questions.q: Who decides whether an English word is "real"?
questions.answer: Nobody and everybody — dictionaries observe usage.

questions.q: What do lexicographers look for?
questions.answer: Words used widely, by many people, in different contexts, over a sustained period.

questions.q: Why won't a word from one viral post be included?
questions.answer: It isn't used widely over time.

questions.q: How is English different from Portuguese and French in this respect?
questions.answer: English has no official academy; its dictionaries are descriptive.

reading.title: Is English being ruined?
reading.text: Complaints about the decline of the English language are almost as old as the language itself. In the eighteenth century, Jonathan Swift lamented the "corruptions" introduced by fashionable young writers and proposed an academy to fix the language once and for all. Two centuries later, critics worried about the influence of American films; more recently, the targets have been text messages, social media and teenagers. Each generation, it seems, is convinced that it is witnessing the end of proper English. Linguists tend to be considerably more relaxed. From their perspective, change is not a sign of decay but a condition of life. Every living language constantly gains new words and loses old ones, shifts its pronunciation and adjusts its grammar. Many words now considered perfectly respectable began as slang or as "errors". "Mob", for example, was once a disreputable abbreviation of the Latin mobile vulgus; "nice" originally meant "foolish"; and the verb "to contact", now indispensable in any office, was widely condemned as vulgar American usage in the early twentieth century. The digital age has undoubtedly accelerated the process. New words can now spread across the globe in days rather than decades, and the boundaries between speech and writing have blurred. Yet research on young people's writing has generally found little evidence that texting damages literacy; some studies even suggest that playful abbreviation requires a sophisticated awareness of how language works. None of this means that every innovation deserves to survive, or that standards no longer matter. Clear, precise language remains essential in law, science and public life, and most speakers are perfectly capable of switching between registers. The real skill, perhaps, is not resisting change but navigating it: knowing when "ghosting" is the perfect word, and when it would be entirely out of place.

questions.q: What did Jonathan Swift propose?
questions.answer: An academy to fix the English language once and for all.

questions.q: How do linguists view language change?
questions.answer: Not as decay but as a normal condition of a living language.

questions.q: Give one example of a word that changed status or meaning.
questions.answer: "Mob" (once disreputable), "nice" (once meant foolish), "to contact" (once considered vulgar).

questions.q: What has research found about texting and literacy?
questions.answer: Little evidence that it damages literacy; it may even show linguistic awareness.

writing.task: Write an essay (300–350 words): "Language change: decline or evolution?" Use examples of neologisms and word formation from English (and, if you wish, Portuguese), and reach a balanced conclusion.
writing.task_pt: Escreva um ensaio (300–350 palavras): "Mudança linguística: declínio ou evolução?" Use exemplos de neologismos e formação de palavras do inglês (e, se quiser, do português) e chegue a uma conclusão equilibrada.
writing.model:
Language change: decline or evolution?

Every few years, a new wave of anxiety sweeps through the media: young people are destroying the language. Their texts are full of abbreviations, their speech full of slang, and words like "ghosting", "adulting" and "doomscrolling" are invading the dictionary. Is this evidence of decline, or simply evolution in action?

There is no doubt that English is changing rapidly. Digital technology has accelerated the creation and spread of new words, many of them formed through familiar processes. Blends such as "staycation" and "infodemic" combine existing words; conversion has turned nouns like "google" and "text" into verbs; and productive suffixes allow speakers to coin terms such as "gamify" or "Uberization" almost effortlessly. Far from being chaotic, these innovations follow patterns that have shaped English for centuries.

Indeed, history suggests that today's "corruption" is often tomorrow's standard. Words such as "mob" and "bus" were once condemned as vulgar abbreviations, and the use of "contact" as a verb provoked indignation in the early twentieth century. Few people would now consider them anything but ordinary English. The same process is visible in Portuguese, which has absorbed words like "deletar" and "printar", to the dismay of some purists.

That said, it would be naive to claim that all change is neutral. Rapidly multiplying jargon can exclude older people or non-specialists, and the informality of online communication can make it harder for some young people to master formal registers when they need them — in job applications, legal documents or academic writing.

The solution, however, is not to resist change but to teach flexibility. A speaker who can use "ghosted" with friends and "failed to respond" in a formal complaint is not a victim of linguistic decline but a skilled user of the language.

In conclusion, language change is neither a catastrophe nor a cause for unqualified celebration. It is, quite simply, what living languages do. Our task is not to stop it, but to understand it — and to use every register well.

culture_note.title: Palavras portuguesas no inglês
culture_note.text_pt: O inglês tomou emprestadas várias palavras do português (algumas via outras línguas): **samba, bossa nova, caipirinha, capoeira, favela, piranha, jaguar, cashew** (de *caju*), **marmalade** (de *marmelada*, via francês) e **flamingo** (provavelmente via português ou espanhol). Por outro lado, o português brasileiro absorveu centenas de anglicismos: **deletar, printar, dar um like, home office**...

grammar.title: Varieties of English
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Britânico x americano** (as diferenças mais comuns):
- **Vocabulário:** flat/apartment, lift/elevator, queue/line, holiday/vacation, pavement/sidewalk, autumn/fall, mobile/cell phone, rubbish/trash, chemist/pharmacy, motorway/highway
- **Ortografia:** colour/color, centre/center, organise/organize (ambos aceitos no UK), travelled/traveled, programme/program, defence/defense
- **Gramática:**
  - **have got** (UK) / **have** (US): "Have you got...?" / "Do you have...?"
  - **Present perfect** mais usado no UK: "I've just eaten" (UK) x "I just ate" (US, comum)
  - **Substantivos coletivos:** "The team **are** playing well" (UK, possível) x "The team **is**..." (US)
  - **Preposições:** at the weekend (UK) / on the weekend (US); different from/to (UK) / different from/than (US)
  - **gotten** (US) / got (UK)
- **Pronúncia:** o "r" final (rhotic no US, non-rhotic em RP: car = "kaa"); o "t" entre vogais (US: water ≈ "wárer"); vogais (bath, can't, tomato)

**2. World Englishes** — variedades legítimas com normas próprias:
- **Inglês indiano:** "do the needful", "prepone" (antecipar, oposto de postpone), "revert" (= responder), "cousin-brother"; uso frequente do contínuo ("I am knowing him")
- **Inglês nigeriano:** "to off the light" (desligar), "to on the TV", "well done" como saudação a quem trabalha
- **Singlish (Singapura):** partículas como **lah**, **lor**, **meh**; "Can or not?", "Got or not?"
- **Inglês sul-africano:** "now-now" (já, já), "just now" (daqui a pouco, às vezes!), "robot" (semáforo)
- **Inglês australiano:** arvo (afternoon), brekkie (breakfast), "no worries"
- **Inglês caribenho/crioulos:** sistemas gramaticais próprios (ex.: Jamaican Patois)

**3. Inglês como língua franca (ELF):** em comunicação internacional, **inteligibilidade** importa mais que sotaque "nativo". Pesquisadores como **Jennifer Jenkins** identificaram um "núcleo" de características de pronúncia que mais afetam a compreensão (certas consoantes, vogais longas x curtas, acento nas palavras importantes) — o resto, como o "th", pode variar sem prejudicar a comunicação.

**4. Atitude C2:** reconheça e **respeite** a variação. Escolha uma variedade-base para escrever (UK ou US) e seja **consistente** na ortografia.

examples.en: In Indian English, "Please revert at the earliest" simply means "Please reply as soon as possible".
examples.pt: No inglês indiano, "Please revert at the earliest" significa simplesmente "Por favor, responda o quanto antes".

grammar.tip_pt: Para melhorar a compreensão de sotaques, **varie suas fontes**: ouça podcasts e entrevistas com falantes da Índia, Nigéria, Escócia, Austrália, Irlanda, África do Sul. Na prova C2 Proficiency, o Listening inclui uma variedade de sotaques.

common_mistakes.why_pt: Consistência ortográfica é esperada em textos formais.

common_mistakes.wrong: Thinking Indian, Nigerian or Singaporean English are "wrong".
common_mistakes.right: They are legitimate varieties with their own norms.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Variação não é erro; é diversidade.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Algumas pistas rápidas: **r final** pronunciado (US, Escócia, Irlanda, Índia) ou não (RP, Austrália, África do Sul); **t entre vogais** como "r" rápido (US, Austrália); **bath / can't** com /ɑː/ longo (sul da Inglaterra) ou /æ/ (US, norte da Inglaterra). Ouça "water", "car" e "bath" em vários sotaques.

dialogue.title: The international team
dialogue.context_pt: Uma reunião online de uma equipe internacional, com membros do Brasil, da Índia, da Escócia e dos EUA.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: Good morning, everyone. Before we start, kindly revert on the budget email at the earliest — I'll do the needful once I have your numbers.
lines.pt: Bom dia a todos. Antes de começarmos, por favor respondam o e-mail do orçamento o quanto antes — farei o necessário assim que tiver os números de vocês.

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.en: Sorry, Priya — "revert"? Do you want us to go back to the old version?
lines.pt: Desculpa, Priya — "revert"? Você quer que a gente volte para a versão antiga?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: Ha, no! In Indian English, "revert" just means "reply". Sorry, I forget that it's not universal.
lines.pt: Ha, não! No inglês indiano, "revert" significa só "responder". Desculpa, esqueço que não é universal.

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: That's interesting. And Jack, earlier you said the meeting had been "preponed"?
lines.pt: Interessante. E Jack, mais cedo você disse que a reunião tinha sido "preponed"?

lines.speaker: Jack
lines.en: No, that was Priya too! I'd say "brought forward". Honestly, I think "prepone" is brilliant — it's the logical opposite of "postpone".
lines.pt: Não, foi a Priya também! Eu diria "brought forward". Sinceramente, acho "prepone" genial — é o oposto lógico de "postpone".

lines.speaker: Mark
lines.en: Speaking of which, I'm in Chicago, so for me the deadline is on the weekend, not at the weekend!
lines.pt: Falando nisso, estou em Chicago, então para mim o prazo é "on the weekend", não "at the weekend"!

lines.speaker: Duda
lines.en: And I'm the Brazilian who learned British English at school and American English from Netflix. I mix everything!
lines.pt: E eu sou a brasileira que aprendeu inglês britânico na escola e americano com a Netflix. Misturo tudo!

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: That's the beauty of it. As long as we understand each other, we're all speaking English.
lines.pt: Essa é a beleza da coisa. Desde que a gente se entenda, todos estamos falando inglês.

listening.title: Whose English is it?
listening.context_pt: Uma pesquisadora fala sobre a expansão global do inglês.

lines.speaker: Researcher
lines.en: The linguist Braj Kachru, who was born in Kashmir and worked in the United States, proposed an influential model of English around the world, often pictured as three concentric circles. The inner circle includes countries where English is the main first language: the UK, the US, Australia and so on. The outer circle includes countries where English has an official or institutional role as a second language, often as a result of colonial history: India, Nigeria, Singapore, the Philippines. And the expanding circle includes countries where English is learned as a foreign language for international communication — Brazil, China, Japan, Germany, and most of the world. The model has been criticized and revised, but its central insight remains powerful: English no longer belongs only to its native speakers. In fact, most interactions in English today probably take place between people for whom it isn't a first language at all. Which raises a fascinating question: who, now, sets the standard?

questions.q: Who proposed the three-circle model?
questions.answer: Braj Kachru.

questions.q: What is the inner circle?
questions.answer: Countries where English is the main first language (UK, US, Australia...).

questions.q: Which circle does Brazil belong to?
questions.answer: The expanding circle.

questions.q: What is the central insight of the model?

reading.title: The myth of the perfect accent
reading.text: For decades, many language learners have pursued a single, elusive goal: to sound like a native speaker. Textbooks offered recordings in "standard" British or American accents; learners practised minimal pairs late into the night; and those who failed to eliminate every trace of their first language often felt that they had, in some sense, failed. In recent years, this ideal has come under sustained criticism. The first problem is practical. There is no single native accent to imitate. A speaker from Glasgow sounds very different from one from London, Dublin, Texas or Sydney, and none of these accents is inherently more correct than the others. Even the "standard" British accent traditionally taught to learners, Received Pronunciation, is spoken natively by only a small minority of people in the United Kingdom. The second problem concerns purpose. For the vast majority of learners, English is a means of communicating with people from many different countries, most of whom are not native speakers themselves. In these situations, what matters is not whether one sounds British or American but whether one is understood. Research on English as a lingua franca has suggested that certain features — word stress, the distinction between some long and short vowels, and a number of consonant sounds — are far more important for intelligibility than others. A Brazilian speaker who pronounces "think" as "fink" will almost always be understood; one who misplaces the stress in "comfortable" or "development" may cause genuine confusion. None of this means that pronunciation does not matter. Clear pronunciation is a courtesy to one's listeners, and many learners find great satisfaction in mastering the sounds of a new language. But the goal has shifted from imitation to intelligibility, and from shame to confidence. An accent, after all, is not a defect. It is a sign that someone has learned to live in more than one language — which is, by any measure, an achievement.

questions.q: What goal have many learners pursued?
questions.answer: To sound like a native speaker.

questions.q: Why is there no single native accent to imitate?
questions.answer: Native accents vary enormously; none is inherently more correct.

questions.q: What matters most in lingua franca communication?
questions.answer: Being understood (intelligibility), not sounding British or American.

questions.q: Which features does research suggest are most important for intelligibility?

writing.model:
Whose English is it anyway?

When I started learning English as a child in Brazil, I believed there was one "correct" version of the language, spoken by people in London or New York, and that my job was to imitate it as closely as possible. Every trace of my Portuguese accent felt like a mistake. It took me many years — and many conversations with people from very different places — to realize how wrong that idea was.

English today is spoken by an estimated one and a half billion people, but only a minority of them learned it as their first language. It is the official or institutional language of countries as diverse as India, Nigeria, Singapore and the Philippines, each of which has developed its own vocabulary, rhythms and expressions. An Indian colleague might ask me to "revert" on an email; a Nigerian friend might ask me to "off the light"; a Singaporean classmate might end a sentence with "lah". These are not errors. They are features of established varieties of English, as legitimate as the British "queue" or the American "sidewalk".

For learners, this has liberating implications. First, there is no single accent we are obliged to imitate. What matters in international communication is intelligibility: speaking clearly, stressing the right syllables and adapting to our listeners. Second, we are not merely visitors in someone else's language. As members of the global community of English users, we have a stake in it — and perhaps even a right to shape it.

That does not mean anything goes. In formal writing, consistency and accuracy still matter, and learners benefit from understanding the major standard varieties. But the old hierarchy, in which native speakers were the only judges of what was correct, is giving way to something more democratic.

So whose English is it? The honest answer is: everyone's who uses it. And that, I believe, is the best reason of all to keep learning it — accent and all.

grammar.title: Modals and expressions of obligation in legal texts
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Shall** — em leis e contratos, expressa **obrigação** ou **determinação legal** (não futuro):
- "The tenant **shall** pay the rent on the first day of each month." (= deve pagar)
- "Everyone **shall** have the right to..." (= terá/tem garantido)
- **Shall not** = proibição: "No one **shall** be held in slavery."
- ⚠️ Muitos especialistas em *plain English* recomendam substituir **shall** por **must** (obrigação) ou pelo presente ("Everyone **has** the right..."), pois "shall" pode ser ambíguo.

**2. Must / must not** — obrigação / proibição clara.

**3. May / may not** — em textos legais:
- **may** = **permissão** ou **possibilidade**: "The landlord **may** inspect the property with 24 hours' notice."
- **may not** = **proibição** (= is not allowed to): "Tenants **may not** sublet the property."

**4. Expressões com be + adjetivo/particípio:**
- **be entitled to** + substantivo/verbo (ter direito a): "Workers **are entitled to** thirty days' leave." / "...entitled to receive..."
- **be liable for** (ser responsável por) / **be liable to** (estar sujeito a — pena, multa): "Offenders **are liable to** a fine of up to..."
- **be obliged / required to** (ser obrigado a)
- **be prohibited / barred / forbidden from** + -ing: "Members **are prohibited from** sharing..."
- **be subject to** (estar sujeito a): "**Subject to** approval" / "Prices **are subject to** change."
- **be eligible for / to** (ser elegível)
- **be exempt from** (ser isento de)

**5. Passiva e linguagem impessoal** — típicas de leis: "It **is hereby** enacted...", "Any person who... **shall be guilty of** an offence."

**6. Explicando em linguagem simples:** "The tenant shall not keep pets" → "You're not allowed to have pets."

examples.en: Under the law, consumers are entitled to cancel online purchases within seven days.
examples.pt: Segundo a lei, os consumidores têm direito a cancelar compras online em até sete dias.

examples.en: Any person who fails to comply with this order shall be liable to a fine.
examples.pt: Qualquer pessoa que descumprir esta ordem estará sujeita a multa.

examples.en: Employees may not disclose confidential information to third parties.
examples.pt: Os funcionários não podem divulgar informações confidenciais a terceiros.

grammar.tip_pt: Atenção: **shall** em contratos **não** é futuro! E **may not** em regulamentos é **proibição**, não "talvez não". Ao ler um contrato em inglês, pergunte sempre: isto é um **direito** (entitled, may), um **dever** (shall, must, required) ou uma **proibição** (shall not, may not, prohibited)?

listening.title: The Universal Declaration
listening.context_pt: Uma professora de direito internacional fala sobre a Declaração Universal dos Direitos Humanos.

lines.speaker: Professor
lines.en: On 10 December 1948, the General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Drafted in the aftermath of the Second World War, it set out, for the first time, a list of rights that all human beings are entitled to, regardless of nationality, race, sex, religion or any other status. The committee that drafted it was chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, and it included representatives from many countries and traditions. Its thirty articles cover civil and political rights — such as the right to life, liberty and a fair trial — as well as economic, social and cultural rights, including the right to education and to work. Notice the language: "No one shall be held in slavery"; "Everyone has the right to education". Technically, the Declaration itself is not a binding treaty. But it has inspired many later legally binding agreements and national constitutions, including Brazil's 1988 Constitution. It has also been translated into more languages than almost any other document in the world.

questions.q: When was the Universal Declaration adopted?
questions.answer: On 10 December 1948.

questions.q: Who chaired the drafting committee?
questions.answer: Eleanor Roosevelt.

questions.q: What two broad types of rights does it cover?
questions.answer: Civil and political rights, and economic, social and cultural rights.

questions.q: Is the Declaration legally binding?
questions.answer: Not itself, but it inspired binding treaties and constitutions.

reading.title: Rights in the digital age
reading.text: When the Universal Declaration of Human Rights was drafted in 1948, its authors could not have imagined smartphones, social media or artificial intelligence. Yet many of the most urgent debates about rights today concern precisely these technologies. Article 12 of the Declaration states that no one shall be subjected to arbitrary interference with their privacy. What does that mean in a world where vast amounts of personal data are collected, analysed and sold, often without users fully understanding what they have agreed to? In response, a growing number of jurisdictions have adopted data protection laws. The European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, which came into force in 2018, has been particularly influential; Brazil's own General Data Protection Law (LGPD) followed shortly afterwards. Under such laws, individuals are typically entitled to know what data is held about them, to request its correction and, in certain circumstances, to have it deleted. Organizations that process data are obliged to have a legal basis for doing so and may be liable to substantial fines if they fail to protect it. New questions continue to emerge. Should people have a right to an explanation when an algorithm denies them a loan or a job? Is internet access itself becoming a basic right, given that so many essential services now depend on it? To what extent should platforms be held liable for harmful content posted by their users? These debates are far from settled. What is clear is that rights are not fixed for all time. They are interpreted, extended and sometimes contested as societies change. The language of the law may sound timeless — "shall", "entitled", "liable" — but the questions it must answer are constantly new.

questions.q: What does Article 12 of the Declaration protect?
questions.answer: Privacy, against arbitrary interference.

questions.q: What rights do individuals typically have under data protection laws?
questions.answer: To know what data is held, request correction and, in some cases, deletion.

questions.q: What may happen to organizations that fail to protect data?
questions.answer: They may be liable to substantial fines.

questions.q: Name one new question about rights in the digital age.
questions.answer: Right to an explanation from algorithms / internet access as a right / platform liability for content.

writing.model:
Charter of Rights and Responsibilities — Riverside Online Learning Community

Preamble
This Charter sets out the rights and responsibilities of all members of the Riverside Online Learning Community ("the Community"). By joining the Community, members agree to abide by its provisions.

Article 1 — Respect
Every member shall have the right to participate in discussions without being subjected to harassment, discrimination or personal attacks. Members shall treat one another with courtesy, regardless of nationality, age, gender, religion or level of English.

Article 2 — Freedom of expression
Members are entitled to express their opinions freely, subject to the limits set out in Article 1. Disagreement is welcome; abuse is not.

Article 3 — Privacy
Members may not share other members' personal information, including photographs, messages or contact details, without their explicit consent. The Community shall not sell or disclose members' data to third parties.

Article 4 — Academic integrity
Members shall submit only their own work. Members found to have plagiarised may be liable to suspension from the Community.

Article 5 — Moderation
Moderators may remove content that breaches this Charter. Any member whose content has been removed shall be entitled to request an explanation and to appeal the decision within fourteen days.

Article 6 — Amendments
This Charter may be amended by a majority vote of members, provided that all members are notified at least one month in advance.

— Plain English summary —
Be respectful: no harassment or discrimination. You can say what you think, but don't attack people. Don't share other people's personal information; we won't sell yours. Only submit your own work — if you copy, you may be suspended. Moderators can delete posts that break the rules, but you can ask why and appeal. Rules can change only if most members vote for it, with a month's notice.

grammar.title: Paraphrasing and synthesizing
grammar.explanation_pt:
**1. Técnicas de paráfrase** (combine várias!):
- **Sinônimos:** "children" → "young people"; "harmful" → "detrimental"
- **Mudar a classe da palavra:** "Technology **has transformed** education" → "Education **has undergone a transformation** because of technology"
- **Mudar a estrutura (ativa/passiva, ordem):** "Schools should ban phones" → "Phones ought to be prohibited in schools"
- **Generalizar / abstrair:** "teachers, parents and pupils" → "the whole school community"
- **Usar um verbo de citação que mostra a posição do autor:** "The writer **contends / warns / dismisses the idea that**..."
⚠️ **Não copie** sequências de 3+ palavras do texto original (exceto termos técnicos).

**2. Resumir:** identifique **a tese** e **2–3 argumentos de cada texto**; ignore exemplos e detalhes.

**3. Sintetizar (comparar os textos):**
- **Concordância:** "Both writers **agree / concur** that..." / "The second text **echoes** this view..."
- **Divergência:** "**Whereas** the first writer..., the second..." / "The second writer **takes issue with**..." / "**Where they diverge** is..."
- **Complemento:** "The second text **adds** a further dimension..." / "...**goes further**, arguing that..."

**4. Avaliar (sua opinião):**
- "I find the first argument **more convincing** because..."
- "**While** the second writer **rightly points out**..., she **overlooks**..."
- "**In my view**, the most persuasive point is..."

**5. Estrutura do essay C2 Part 1 (240–280 palavras):**
1. **Introdução:** tema geral + o que os dois textos discutem
2. **Texto 1:** ideias principais (parafraseadas) + sua avaliação
3. **Texto 2:** ideias principais + relação com o texto 1 + sua avaliação
4. **Conclusão:** sua posição geral
(Alternativa: organizar por **temas**, comparando os dois textos em cada parágrafo.)

rows: Social media is harmful to teenagers.
Young people's well-being may be damaged by online platforms.
Mobile devices ought to be prohibited in classrooms.
Education has undergone a profound transformation as a result of technology.
This view is far from universally accepted.
It costs a lot of money.

examples.en: Both writers concur that remote work offers greater flexibility; where they diverge is in their assessment of its long-term impact on collaboration.
examples.pt: Os dois autores concordam que o trabalho remoto oferece mais flexibilidade; onde divergem é na avaliação de seu impacto de longo prazo na colaboração.

examples.en: The second writer takes issue with the idea that technology alone can solve educational inequality.
examples.pt: O segundo autor contesta a ideia de que a tecnologia sozinha pode resolver a desigualdade educacional.

examples.en: In a nutshell, the first text is optimistic, the second cautious — and the truth, I would argue, lies somewhere in between.
examples.pt: Em poucas palavras, o primeiro texto é otimista, o segundo cauteloso — e a verdade, eu diria, está em algum ponto intermediário.

grammar.tip_pt: Na prova, **planeje 10 minutos**: sublinhe a tese e os argumentos de cada texto, anote **sinônimos** antes de escrever e decida sua opinião. O erro mais comum é **copiar frases inteiras** do texto — isso é penalizado. O segundo mais comum é **esquecer a avaliação**.

common_mistakes.wrong: Copying full sentences from the input texts.
common_mistakes.right: Paraphrase using synonyms, new structures and reporting verbs.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Na prova, cópia de trechos é penalizada.

common_mistakes.right: Include your opinion on each text and an overall position.
common_mistakes.why_pt: A tarefa exige resumo E avaliação.

common_mistakes.wrong: Including examples and minor details from the texts.
common_mistakes.right: Focus on the main arguments only.
common_mistakes.why_pt: Com 240–280 palavras, não há espaço para detalhes.

pronunciation.tip_pt: Ao resumir um texto em voz alta (numa reunião, por exemplo), use **marcadores claros** e **pausas** entre as ideias: "So, in a nutshell, | the first report says... | The second, by contrast, | argues that... | Where they agree is...". Acentue as palavras de **contraste**.
practice: In a NUTshell, | BOTH writers agree that...
The SECond, by CONtrast, | argues that...
Where they diVERGE | is in the SOlution.

dialogue.title: Briefing the boss
dialogue.context_pt: Uma analista resume dois relatórios para o diretor antes de uma reunião.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.en: I've got five minutes before the board meeting. Can you give me the gist of those two reports on the four-day week?
lines.pt: Tenho cinco minutos antes da reunião do conselho. Pode me dar a ideia geral daqueles dois relatórios sobre a semana de quatro dias?

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: Sure. In a nutshell: the first, from the consultancy, is very positive. It argues that a shorter week boosts productivity and reduces burnout, and it recommends a company-wide trial.
lines.pt: Claro. Em poucas palavras: o primeiro, da consultoria, é muito positivo. Argumenta que uma semana mais curta aumenta a produtividade e reduz o burnout, e recomenda um teste em toda a empresa.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.en: And the second?
lines.pt: E o segundo?

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: The finance team's report takes issue with that. It doesn't dispute the well-being benefits, but it warns that customer service could suffer, especially in our call centres.
lines.pt: O relatório da equipe financeira contesta isso. Não questiona os benefícios para o bem-estar, mas alerta que o atendimento ao cliente pode sofrer, principalmente nas nossas centrais.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.en: So where do they agree?
lines.pt: E onde eles concordam?

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: Both concur that staff are exhausted and that something needs to change. Where they diverge is on the solution — and the risk.
lines.pt: Ambos concordam que a equipe está exausta e que algo precisa mudar. Onde divergem é na solução — e no risco.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.en: What's your view?
lines.pt: Qual é sua opinião?

lines.speaker: Juliana
lines.en: I think the second report strikes a better balance. My suggestion would be a six-month trial in two departments first — not the whole company.
lines.pt: Acho que o segundo relatório encontra um equilíbrio melhor. Minha sugestão seria um teste de seis meses em dois departamentos primeiro — não na empresa toda.

lines.speaker: Director
lines.en: Perfect. That's exactly what I needed. Thank you.
lines.pt: Perfeito. Era exatamente o que eu precisava. Obrigado.

listening.title: Two views on homework
listening.context_pt: Dois especialistas apresentam visões diferentes sobre lição de casa num programa de rádio.

lines.speaker: Voice 1
lines.en: Homework, in my view, remains an essential part of learning. It reinforces what students have studied in class, develops independent study habits and gives parents a window into their children's education. Without it, many pupils would simply forget what they had learned. The problem is not homework itself but bad homework: repetitive tasks that take hours and teach nothing new.

lines.speaker: Voice 2
lines.en: I'd go further. The research on homework, particularly for younger children, is mixed at best. Some studies suggest a modest benefit for older students, but for primary school pupils, the evidence is weak. Meanwhile, homework can increase stress and inequality: children with educated parents and quiet places to study benefit, while others fall further behind. I'd abolish it for under-twelves and drastically reduce it for everyone else.

questions.q: What does the first speaker think homework is good for?
questions.answer: Reinforcing learning, developing study habits and involving parents.

questions.q: What does the first speaker see as the real problem?
questions.answer: Bad homework — repetitive, time-consuming and not useful.

questions.q: What does the second speaker say about the research?
questions.answer: It's mixed; weak evidence for young children, some benefit for older students.

questions.q: Where do the speakers agree and diverge? (synthesis)
questions.answer: Both criticize bad/excessive homework; they diverge on whether homework is essential (1) or should be abolished for young children (2).

reading.title: C2 Part 1 practice: two texts on tourism
reading.text:
Text 1 — The case for tourism
For many regions, tourism is not merely an industry but a lifeline. It brings income to places where few other opportunities exist, creates jobs for young people who might otherwise be forced to migrate, and provides funding for the preservation of historic buildings and natural landscapes. Moreover, travel broadens the mind: visitors who encounter other cultures at first hand often return home more tolerant and curious. To condemn tourism wholesale, as some critics now do, is to ignore the livelihoods of millions and the very real benefits of human contact across borders.

Text 2 — The cost of popularity
Across the world, a growing number of cities and natural sites are struggling under the weight of their own popularity. In some historic centres, short-term rentals have driven up housing costs so steeply that local residents can no longer afford to live there; neighbourhoods once full of life now resemble theme parks. Fragile ecosystems are damaged by crowds, and much of the money generated by tourism flows to international companies rather than local communities. This is not an argument against travel itself, but against an unregulated model that treats places as products. Without limits, tourism risks destroying the very things that make destinations worth visiting.

Model essay
Both texts address the impact of tourism on the places that receive it, but they reach rather different conclusions.

The first writer presents tourism as vital for many communities, arguing that it generates income and employment in areas with few alternatives and helps finance the conservation of heritage and nature. The text also emphasizes the cultural value of travel, suggesting that contact with other ways of life fosters open-mindedness. While these points are undoubtedly valid, the writer arguably overstates the case by dismissing critics so readily.

The second text, by contrast, focuses on the consequences of excessive tourism. Its author contends that soaring demand for holiday accommodation has priced residents out of their own neighbourhoods, that natural environments are suffering, and that the economic benefits often bypass local people. Crucially, however, the writer does not reject travel as such, but rather a model that lacks regulation.

In my view, the second text offers the more nuanced analysis. It acknowledges, at least implicitly, the advantages highlighted in the first text, while identifying real problems that a purely positive account ignores. The challenge, as I see it, is not to choose between tourism and its critics, but to strike a balance: to welcome visitors while ensuring that communities retain control over their homes, their environment and their economy.

questions.q: What are the main arguments of Text 1?
questions.answer: Tourism provides income and jobs, funds preservation and broadens the mind.

questions.q: What are the main arguments of Text 2?
questions.answer: Overtourism raises housing costs, damages ecosystems and benefits international companies more than locals; it needs regulation.

questions.q: Find two paraphrases in the model essay.
questions.answer: Examples: "priced residents out" (local residents can no longer afford...); "bypass local people" (flows to international companies); "fosters open-mindedness" (broadens the mind).

questions.q: What is the writer's own evaluation?
questions.answer: Text 2 is more nuanced; the solution is to strike a balance through regulation.

writing.model:
Homework: essential or outdated?

The value of homework has long divided educators and parents, and the two contributions considered here illustrate the debate well.

The first speaker defends homework as a fundamental component of education. In her view, tasks completed at home consolidate classroom learning, encourage pupils to work independently and allow families to follow their children's progress. Importantly, she acknowledges that much homework is poorly designed, attributing the problem not to the practice itself but to repetitive, time-consuming assignments that add little to students' understanding. This distinction seems to me a sensible one, although she offers little evidence to support her confidence in homework's benefits.

The second speaker takes a considerably more sceptical position. Drawing on research, he argues that the advantages of homework are, at best, uncertain, particularly in primary education. Furthermore, he raises the important issue of fairness: pupils from more privileged homes, he contends, are far better placed to benefit from work set outside school, so homework may actually widen educational gaps. His proposal — to eliminate homework for younger children and greatly reduce it for older ones — follows logically from this analysis.

On balance, I find the second argument more persuasive, largely because it addresses the question of equity, which the first speaker overlooks. That said, both contributions converge on one crucial point: the quantity and quality of homework matter far more than whether it exists at all. A reasonable compromise, I would suggest, might be to limit homework to short, purposeful tasks — such as reading — for younger pupils, while ensuring that schools provide quiet study spaces for those who lack them at home.

culture_note.title: Resumo no ENEM e no exterior
culture_note.text_pt: No Brasil, a habilidade de resumir aparece em provas como o ENEM (interpretação de textos) e em vestibulares. Em universidades anglófonas, o **summary** e o **critical review** são tarefas acadêmicas constantes, e **plágio** (inclusive copiar frases sem aspas) é tratado com muita seriedade — podendo levar à reprovação ou expulsão. Parafrasear bem é, portanto, uma questão de **integridade acadêmica**.
